This improves the $\widetilde{O}_{\varepsilon,\log n}(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}$ $\min(d,\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}))$ query algorithm of [Beretta et al., SODA 2026] that has access to Degree, Neighbour, and RandEdge queries. We show that any algorithm that has access to Degree, Neighbour, and RandEdge queries, must make at least $\Omega\left(\min\left(d,\frac{\alpha}{d}\right)\right)$ queries, even with the knowledge of $n$ and $\alpha$. Even with Pair and FullNbr queries, an algorithm must make $\Omega\left(\min\left(d,\frac{\alpha}{d}\right)\right)$ queries for certain ranges of $\alpha$. When $n$ is unknown, any algorithm with access to all the queries discussed above must make $\Omega\left(\min\left(d,\frac{\alpha}{d}\right)\right)$ queries. We also establish that any sublinear algorithm using Degree and RandEdge queries must make at least $\Omega(\frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ RandEdge queries. Furthermore, any algorithm having access to Degree, FullNbr, and RandEdge queries that makes $o(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2})$ RandEdge queries must make $\Omega(\frac{\alpha}{\varepsilon^2d})$ Degree and FullNbr queries. This settles the query complexity of estimating average degree using Degree and FullNbr queries.
item.dc:creator: Debarshi Chanda

item.title: Publishing Below-Threshold Triangle Counts under Local Weight Differential Privacy
item.description: arXiv:2601.01710v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose an algorithm for counting below-threshold triangles in weighted graphs under local weight differential privacy. While prior work has largely focused on unweighted graphs, edge weights are intrinsic to many real-world networks. We consider the setting in which the graph topology is publicly known and privacy is required only for the contribution of an individual to incident edge weights, capturing practical scenarios such as road and telecommunication networks. Our method uses two rounds of communication. In the first round, each node releases privatized information about its incident edge weights under local weight differential privacy. In the second round, nodes locally count below-threshold triangles using this privatized information; we introduce both biased and unbiased variants of the estimator. We further develop two refinements: (i) a pre-computation step that reduces covariance and thus lowers expected error, and (ii) an efficient procedure for computing smooth sensitivity, which substantially reduces running time relative to a straightforward implementation. Finally, we present experimental results that quantify the trade-offs between the biased and unbiased variants and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed improvements.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Pfisterer, Quentin Hillebrand, Vorapong Suppakitpaisarn

item.title: Near-Linear Time Computation of Welzl Orders on Graphs with Linear Neighborhood Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2602.14625v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Orders with low crossing number, introduced by Welzl, are a fundamental tool in range searching and computational geometry. Recently, they have found important applications in structural graph theory: set systems with linear shatter functions correspond to graph classes with linear neighborhood complexity. For such set systems S = (U, F), Welzl's theorem guarantees the existence of orders with only O(log^2 n) crossings, n = |U|. A series of works has progressively improved the runtime for computing such orders, from Chazelle and Welzl's original O(|U|^3 |F|) bound (Chazelle and Welzl, 1989), through Har-Peled's O(|U|^2|F|) (Har-Peled, 2009), to the recent sampling-based methods of Csik\'os and Mustafa (Csik\'os and Mustafa, 2024). We present a randomized algorithm that computes Welzl orders for set systems with linear primal and dual shatter functions in expected time O(||S|| log ||S||), where ||S|| = |U| + sum_{X in F} |X| is the size of the canonical input representation. The algorithm achieves an asymptotically optimal O(log n) crossing bound. As an application, we compute compact neighborhood covers in graph classes with (near-)linear neighborhood complexity in time O((n+m) log n), where n and m are the numbers of vertices and edges. Our result also improves the runtime of first-order model checking on monadically stable graph classes from O(n^(5+epsilon)) to O(n^(3+epsilon)).
item.dc:creator: Jan Dreier, Clemens Kuske

item.title: Intermittent Cauchy walks enable optimal 3D search across target shapes and sizes
item.description: arXiv:2603.10655v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Efficiently locating rare targets requires balancing the exploration of novel space with the exploitation of local vicinities. While this tradeoff is well-documented in simplified environments, its behavior in realistic three-dimensional environments remains unclear. Here we analyze intermittent L\'evy walks in three dimensions and show that search efficiency becomes strongly dependent on target geometry, with volume, surface area, and elongation governing performance across the L\'evy spectrum. Against this geometric complexity, the Cauchy walk ($\mu = 2$) emerges as a robust, near-optimal solution across a wide range of target geometries. Specifically, we prove that for convex targets of surface area $\Delta$ in a domain of volume $n$, the optimal expected detection time scales as $n/\Delta$, and that the Cauchy walk achieves this scaling up to polylogarithmic factors, while other L\'evy strategies are suboptimal in different geometric regimes. Our findings provide a theoretical framework for biological movement patterns, including marine predator foraging and immune surveillance, and inform the design of efficient search algorithms for engineered systems such as autonomous nanoscale explorers.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Stromieri, Emanuele Natale, Amos Korman

item.title: Non-Exclusive Notifications for Ride-Hailing at Lyft I: Single-Cycle Approximation Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2603.21533v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms increasingly rely on non-exclusive notifications--broadcasting a single request to multiple drivers simultaneously--to mitigate inefficiencies caused by uncertain driver acceptance. In this paper, the first in a two-part collaboration with Lyft, we formally model the Notification Set Selection Problem for a single decision cycle, where the platform determines the optimal subset of drivers to notify for each incoming ride request. We analyze this combinatorial optimization problem under two contention-resolution protocols: First Acceptance (FA), which prioritizes speed by assigning the ride to the first responder, and Best Acceptance (BA), which prioritizes match quality by selecting the highest-valued accepting driver. We show that welfare maximization under both mechanisms is NP-hard, ruling out a polynomial-time exact algorithm unless P=NP. Despite this hardness, we establish several positive algorithmic results. For FA, we develop a Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS) for the single-rider problem. For the general matching setting, we provide a (1-1/e)-approximation algorithm that applies to both FA and BA. Along the way, we show that the FA valuation function constitutes a novel discrete choice model with structural properties of independent interest. For BA, we further prove that the welfare objective is monotone and submodular and exploit additional structure to obtain an approximation guarantee that surpasses the classical (1-1/e) barrier. Finally, when acceptance probabilities are independent of the drivers, we show that the BA problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time through a linear programming formulation. We evaluate our algorithms on synthetic instances and on instances calibrated using real ride-sharing data from Lyft, demonstrating strong empirical performance.
item.dc:creator: Farbod Ekbatani, Rad Niazadeh, Shruti Penumatsa, Mehdi Golari, Romain Camilleri, Titouan Jehl, Chris Sholley, Matthew Leventi, Theresa Calderon, Angela Lam, Paul Havard Duclos, Tim Holland, James Koch, Shreya Reddy

item.title: String Representation Based on Substring Equation Systems
item.description: arXiv:2604.04377v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Repetitiveness measures quantify how much repetitive structure a string contains and serve as parameters for compressed representations and indexing data structures. Many compression schemes represent strings by recording equalities between identical substrings. We study string compression based on substring equation systems (SESs), which represent strings as unique solutions to substring-equality and character-assignment constraints. We show that every string $w$ has an SES of size $O(\chi(w))$, where $\chi(w)$ is the size of a smallest suffixient set for $w$ with a unique terminal symbol appended. This result establishes the reachability of $\chi$, which had been an open problem. We also prove that computing the size $s(w)$ of the smallest SES that represents $w$ is NP-hard and $(1 + \varepsilon)$-inapproximable for some fixed constant $\varepsilon > 0$. Finally, we prove that the size $b(w)$ of the smallest bidirectional macro scheme (BMS) representing $w$ satisfies $s(w) \leq b(w) \leq 4s(w)$. Hence, SES and BMS are equivalent up to a constant factor, and this equivalence gives the new bound $b(w) \in O(\chi(w))$.
item.dc:creator: Hiroki Shibata, Hideo Bannai

item.title: Asymptotically Faster Algorithms for Recognizing $(k,\ell)$-Sparse Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2604.13025v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For fixed integers $k,\ell$ with $0\leq\ell<3k$, we study the problem of deciding whether a graph is $(k,\ell)$-sparse, a notion arising in combinatorial optimization and rigidity theory. Standard pebble-game algorithms take $O(n^2)$ time for $0\leq\ell<2k$ and $O(n^3)$ time for $2k\leq\ell<3k$, although faster algorithms were known for some parameter choices. We develop efficient recognition algorithms using bounded-indegree orientations, reductions to rooted arc-connectivity, augmenting paths, and centroid decomposition. For $0\leq\ell<2k$, they run in $O(n^{1+o(1)})$ time, yielding the first subquadratic bound valid throughout the entire range. Purely combinatorial implementations run in $O(n\sqrt n)$ time throughout this range. For graphs with $O(n)$ edges, we also improve the purely combinatorial running time for decomposing the edge set into a fixed number of forests, or certifying that no such decomposition exists, from $O(n\sqrt{n\log n})$ to $O(n\sqrt n)$. For simple graphs with $2k\leq\ell<3k$, the general recognition algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time when $\ell\leq2k+2$ and in $O(n^2\log n)$ time otherwise. When $\ell=2k$ and $k\leq3$, a specialized algorithm improves this to $O(n^{1+o(1)})$ and admits a purely combinatorial $O(n\sqrt n)$ implementation. Whenever the input graph is not $(k,\ell)$-sparse, our recognition algorithms return an explicit violating vertex set.
item.dc:creator: Bence De\'ak, P\'eter Madarasi

item.title: Parameterized Capacitated Vertex Cover Revisited
item.description: arXiv:2604.18746v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Capacitated Vertex Cover is a generalization of Vertex Cover where we seek a set of $k$ vertices covering all edges, but with the added constraint that for each vertex we are given a capacity, that is, a maximum number of incident edges the vertex can cover if selected. This problem is well-studied in parameterized complexity and is known to be in XP but W[1]-hard parameterized by treewidth. Natural dynamic programs lead to complexities of the form $C^{\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{tw})}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, $\Delta^{\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{tw})}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, or $k^{\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{tw})}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, where $C, \Delta$ are respectively the maximum capacity and maximum degree. These results imply an FPT algorithm for parameter $k$ with complexity $k^{\mathcal{O}(k)}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, as $\mathrm{tw}\le k$. These simple dynamic programming algorithms essentially constitute the state of the art. Our main question is therefore whether these algorithms can be improved. We address this question from numerous angles...
item.dc:creator: Michael Lampis, Manolis Vasilakis

item.title: A Polynomial Kernel for Vertex Deletion to the Scattered Class of Proper Interval Graph and Trees
item.description: arXiv:2605.02399v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vertex deletion to the hereditary graph class has been well-studied in parameterized complexity. Vertex deletion in scattered graph classes has attracted attention in recent years. In this paper, we consider (PROPER-INTERVAL, TREE)-VERTEX DELETION, the input to which is an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ and an integer $k$. The goal is to pick a set $X \subseteq V(G)$ with at most $k$ vertices such that $G - X$ is a simple graph and every connected component of $G - X$ is a proper interval graph or a tree. When parameterized by the solution size $k$, (PROPER-INTERVAL, TREE)-VERTEX DELETION has been proved to be fixed-parameter tractable by Jacob et al. [JCSS-2023, FCT-2021]. Notably, (PROPER-INTERVAL, TREE)-VERTEX DELETION is a natural and substantial generalization of (CLIQUE, TREE)-VERTEX DELETION, which has been explored recently [JCSS-2026, ISAAC-2025, IPL-2025, ISAAC-2024]. The kernelization techniques for the latter exploit the finite forbidden induced subgraph characterization of cliques. In contrast, proper interval graphs and trees admit infinite forbidden induced subgraph characterizations, requiring new structural arguments. In this paper, we consider this problem from the perspective of polynomial kernelization and provide the first nontrivial polynomial kernel for (PROPER-INTERVAL, TREE)-VERTEX DELETION, with $O(k^{33})$ vertices.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Jacob, Arpit Kumar, Diptapriyo Majumdar

item.title: An Evaluation of Vertex Elimination Strategies for Algorithmic Differentiation
item.description: arXiv:2605.24280v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The algorithmic differentiation (AD) of mathematical functions can be interpreted as a sequence of vertex eliminations in an underlying directed acyclic graph. The problem of determining a minimum-cost elimination ordering, which we call Optimal Vertex Elimination, is NP-complete, and much effort has been devoted to the design of heuristics. Many of these heuristics are widely believed to perform well in practice, but this hypothesis has so far been difficult to test due to the lack of scalable exact methods. We design and engineer new integer programming formulations for Optimal Vertex Elimination and for a related objective we call Minimum Edge Count. Our implementations scale to graphs one-to-two orders of magnitude larger than existing techniques, facilitating the assembly of a corpus of medium-sized graphs for which optimal solutions are known. We give a comprehensive evaluation of existing heuristics on this corpus. We also make several theoretical contributions, including a tight analysis of the forward and reverse modes of AD, a simple algorithm for Optimal Vertex Elimination with approximation ratio parameterized by the size of a minimum source-sink separator, and the first approximation lower bounds for both problems.
item.dc:creator: Alex Crane, P{\aa}l Gr{\o}n{\aa}s Drange, Eli Friedman, Paul D. Hovland, Jan H\"uckelheim, Andrew Lyons, Yosuke Mizutani, Mac\'eo Ottavy, Blair D. Sullivan

item.title: Optimal Extrapolation Bounds for Sparse Fourier Sums
item.dc:creator: Ruizhe Zhang

item.title: Near-Optimal In-Place Sorting
item.description: arXiv:2607.27040v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an in-place comparison-based sorting algorithm that sorts an array of $n$ elements using $n\lg n + O(n)$ comparisons with exponentially high probability and always $O(n)$ moves. This serves as the first in-place sorting algorithm to match the fundamental $n\lg n+O(n)$ lower bound on total operations (i.e. sum of comparisons and moves). For the worst-case, we present an algorithm that makes $n\lg n + O(n\lg^{(t)}n)$ comparisons and $O(tn)$ data moves, where $t$ is an integer parameter satisfying $2 \leq t \leq \lg^{*}n - 1$ and $\lg^{(t)}n$ denotes the $t$-time iterated logarithm, improving over the previous upper bound of $n\lg n + O(n\lg\lg n)$ comparisons and $O(n)$ moves when using constant $t>2$. When $t\approx \lg^* n$, this yields a worst-case upper bound on total operations of $n\lg n+O(n \lg^* n)$. We thus achieve the ultimate goal of efficient in-place sorting via randomization whilst narrowing the gap to this goal in the worst-case. This advance involves a novel ordered set structure that supports searches in an optimal $\lg n + O(1)$ comparisons for $n$ elements. Note that both algorithms are unstable.
item.dc:creator: Alex Zihan Xu, Stephen Jing Chick

item.title: A Tight Bound for Facial Distance Patterns in Planar Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2608.07187v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Let $G$ be an undirected unweighted planar graph and let $S=(s_0,\dots,s_{k-1})$ be the vertices of a designated face, listed in cyclic order. Consider a vector that stores the distances from an arbitrary vertex $v$ to all vertices of $S$. The pattern of $v$ is obtained by taking the difference between every pair of consecutive values in this vector. Li and Parter [STOC'19] proved an upper bound of $O(k^3)$ on the number of unique patterns over all vertices of $G$. We improve this to $O(k^2)$, matching a known lower bound and settling a conjecture in [ISAAC'22]. The simple proof was found by OpenAI's GPT 5.6-Sol model. Plugging this new bound into known results has the following three immediate implications for undirected unweighted planar graphs: (1) it gives an improved compression of the Okamura-Seymour metric (2) it improves the space required by constant-time exact distance oracles, and (3) it improves the fastest distributed algorithm for computing the diameter. We further present a previously unknown and nontrivial implication: a (centralized) $\tilde{O}(n^{8/5})$-time algorithm for computing the diameter, improving over the $\tilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ algorithm of [SODA'18] which works for weighted directed planar graphs. Thus, there is currently a gap between the time for computing the diameter between weighted and unweighted planar graphs.
item.dc:creator: Viktor Fredslund-Hansen, Shay Mozes, Oren Weimann

item.title: The Cost of Changing Edges for Diameter Computation and More
item.description: arXiv:2608.12628v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The sensitivity setting is a restricted setting for dynamic algorithms, particularly practical for scenarios where extensive preprocessing is feasible but responses to real-time modifications must be near-instantaneous before the data structure is eventually rebuilt. For graph problems, a sensitivity data structure is constructed with a preprocessing time P so that the following queries can be answered quickly, preferably in $O(1)$ time: given an edge $e$, return the answer to the problem on either $G \setminus e$ (decremental) or $G \cup e$ (incremental). We almost entirely settle the decremental setting for the diameter and eccentricities problems in a variety of approximation regimes by matching P to the static runtime while supporting $O(1)$-time queries, thereby improving upon all previous single-failure results [Bil\'o, Cohen, Friedrich, Schirneck, MFCS 2021; Bil\'o, Choudhary, Cohen, Friedrich, Krogmann, Schirneck, ICALP 2023, Algorithmica 2026]. More precisely: (1) We provide a tight reduction demonstrating that any exact distance sensitivity oracle can be used to efficiently solve decremental exact diameter and all-node eccentricities; (2) For the approximate setting, we match the runtime of all known static diameter algorithms across all sparsity settings, up to an additional $1+o(1)$ factor in approximation. Conversely, for the previously unexplored incremental setting of these problems: (3) We develop new lower bounds, demonstrating that no incremental algorithm can efficiently approximate diameter, radius, or eccentricity beyond a $5/3$ factor in undirected graphs or a $2$ factor in directed graphs; (4) We introduce two new instructive techniques and demonstrate how to utilize them to construct several new algorithms. Most notably, we develop incremental single-node eccentricity approximations for both directed and undirected graphs that match our new lower bounds.
item.dc:creator: Sam Hiken, Yael Kirkpatrick, Jakob Nogler, Virginia Vassilevska Williams

item.title: A Simple Algorithm for the Directed Multiple Source Replacement Paths Problem
item.description: arXiv:2608.16615v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the replacement paths (RP) problem, we are given a graph $G = (V, E)$ with $n = |V|$ and $m = |E|$, together with two vertices $s, t \in V$, and are asked to compute the shortest-path distance from $s$ to $t$ in $G \setminus e$ for every failed edge $e \in E$. The multiple source replacement paths (MSRP) problem is its natural generalization: given a set $S \subseteq V$ of $\sigma$ sources, compute the replacement path distances for all pairs in $S \times V$. In this paper, we present a randomized combinatorial algorithm that solves MSRP on unweighted directed graphs in $\tilde{O}(m\sqrt{\sigma n} + \sigma n^2)$ time, with all the output distances correct with high probability. This improves the best known bound $\tilde{O}(m\min\{\sigma\sqrt{n}, n\} + \sigma n^2)$ for directed graphs, which is obtained either by running the single source RP algorithm of Chechik and Magen [ICALP'20] from each source separately or by constructing and querying the all-pairs distance sensitivity oracle of Bernstein and Karger [STOC'09]. Our running time is essentially tight among combinatorial algorithms because Gupta, Jain, and Modi [PODC'20] proved a lower bound of $m{(\sigma n)}^{1/2-o(1)}$ for such algorithms, which holds even on undirected graphs, and the additive term $\sigma n^2$ is proportional to the time needed to write down the $\Theta(\sigma n^2)$ output distances. The algorithm is also remarkably simple.
item.dc:creator: Kaito Harada, Taisuke Izumi

item.title: Approximating the Rural Postman Problem below 3/2
item.description: arXiv:2608.27607v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give an approximation algorithm for the rural postman problem with approximation ratio strictly smaller than $3/2$. We obtain this result by adapting to the rural postman problem the technique of sampling from maximum entropy distributions for the metric traveling salesman problem of Karlin, Klein, and Oveis Gharan. We also observe that, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, any $\alpha$-approximation algorithm for the metric traveling salesman problem yields an $(\alpha+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for the rural postman problem; this implication is already implicit in the treatment of edges that must be traversed in the work of Lampis on the inapproximability of the traveling salesman problem.
item.dc:creator: Hong Li, Jianping Li, Wei Li, Runtao Xie, Xiaoxiao Yang

item.title: Dense Weak Hiding: Closing Complexity Gaps in Nonconvex and PL Finite-Sum Optimization under Individual Smoothness
item.description: arXiv:2609.00045v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Under individual smoothness, known algorithms for nonconvex finite-sum optimization use $O(n+\sqrt n\Delta L_{\max}/\varepsilon^2)$ incremental first-order oracle (IFO) calls, while existing lower bounds miss the factor $\sqrt n$ in the second term. We prove the matching lower bound $\Omega(n+\sqrt n\Delta L_{\max}/\varepsilon^2)$ for randomized IFO algorithms, allowing component indices and query points to depend on the complete preceding history. Thus PAGE and SPIDER are minimax optimal up to universal constants under individual and mean-squared smoothness. Under the global Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition, prior lower bounds did not capture the correct dependence on $n$ under individual smoothness, and the regime of small $\kappa$ remained open for randomized IFO algorithms. We prove an $\Omega(n+\kappa_{\max}\sqrt n\log(\Delta/\varepsilon))$ lower bound for $\kappa_{\max}\ge\sqrt n$, and an $\Omega(n+n\log(\Delta/\varepsilon)/(1+\log(\sqrt n/\kappa_{\max})))$ lower bound for $3\le\kappa_{\max}\le\sqrt n$. Restarted PAGE attains matching upper bounds under mean-squared smoothness in terms of $\kappa_{\rm ms}=L_{\rm ms}/\mu$. Our lower bounds use dense weak hiding. Each hidden direction is spread across all components, making individual queries weakly informative while preserving the direction in the average. A sufficiently large dimension makes premature activation of future stages unlikely within the query budget. Balancing the cost of revealing a stage against the number of stages permitted by individual smoothness yields the missing $\sqrt n$ factor.
item.dc:creator: Yuxing Peng, Zhiqing Tang, Weijia Jia

item.title: Reportable Shortcuts with RLBWTs
item.description: arXiv:2609.06596v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Backward search over a run-length compressed Burrows--Wheeler transform (RLBWT) takes one step per pattern character, even when long stretches of the pattern match material that recurs throughout a highly repetitive collection. We describe \emph{shortcuts}: for a precomputed set of pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ of strings, a backward search that has just matched $\beta$ and finds $\alpha$ immediately to its left in the pattern can cross $\alpha$ in one step. Since a shortcut is taken only after its pair has been recognized in the pattern, the search can record it, and it returns a report of the shortcuts it took along with the usual BWT interval. Our motivation is pangenome graphs, where such pairs mark the places where a pattern passes through a vertex. We work out the case of a single linear reference $\Rref$, in which $\beta$ ranges over the length-$\ell$ windows of $\Rref$ starting at multiples of $\ell$, and $\alpha$ over the $2^t \ell$ characters of $\Rref$ preceding such a window. We show that the resulting search counts correctly; that it crosses a stretch of the pattern matching $m$ consecutive windows of $\Rref$, whose anchors were all kept, with $O(\log m + m / 2^\tau)$ shortcuts, where $2^\tau \ell$ is the longest shortcut, provided the stretch and the rest of the pattern to its right occur together in the collection; and that the shortcuts can be built from the RLBWT in $O(|\Rref| (\tau + 1) \log r)$ time plus $O(\log n)$ time per BWT row they cover, plus the time to sort the anchors. On the 461-megabyte Pizza\&Chili \texttt{cere} collection of 37 genomes, shortcuts make backward search $2.3$ to $4.2$ times faster on exact patterns of length 200 to 1000, and $1.7$ to $2.0$ times faster on patterns with 1\% of their characters substituted, for 86\% more space than the RLBWT.
item.dc:creator: Travis Gagie

item.title: Toward Optimal Time-Space Tradeoffs for Set Reconciliation
item.description: arXiv:2609.14442v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Set reconciliation, where two parties each holding a large set of elements aim to identify their set difference, is a fundamental task in many areas. Time (computation cost) and space (communication cost) are two important metrics in this problem, and much existing work optimizes one at the expense of the other, creating a clear trade-off. We study this trade-off through algorithmic upper bounds and matching space lower bounds. On one side, we propose XYZ-Sketch. For sufficiently large $d$, XYZ-Sketch achieves high-probability reconciliation for sets whose differing elements are uniformly random, using only $(1+\varepsilon)d$ elements for communication, while achieving $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ insertion time and expected $O(d\log V\log^{3/2}(1/\varepsilon))$ decoding time, where $d$ and $V$ denote the size of the difference between two sets and the universe size, respectively. On the other side, we establish a broad fixed-support canonical model and prove a matching space lower bound, establishing the asymptotic optimality of XYZ-Sketch. Our proof also establishes an extremality theorem resolving Walzer's conjecture. Experiments demonstrate the practical advantages of XYZ-Sketch, and the source code is available at https://github.com/djwj233/XYZ-Sketch.
item.dc:creator: Rui Xu, Kangyang Zhou, Jiachen Xu, Jiarui Guo, Boyu Xian, Kaicheng Yang, Yong Cui, Tong Yang

item.title: Move-rb: Faster Bi-Directional r-indexes and Approximate Pattern Matching
item.description: arXiv:2609.30089v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Approximate pattern matching (APM) on highly repetitive texts is a central task in bioinformatics. Bi-directional r-indexes support left- and right-extension of a pattern and thereby accelerate APM algorithms based on search schemes, but existing variants -- br-index and b-move -- suffer from two bottlenecks: $O(\sigma)$ character-predecessor/-successor queries on the run-length-encoded BWT per extension, and predecessor queries on sparse bit vectors to maintain a value in the suffix array interval and to access the PLCP array while locating. We present Move-rb, a bi-directional r-index built on the optimized r-index Move-r. Although Move-rb is 2x larger than br-index, it is up to 24% smaller than b-move, answers APM queries 1-4 orders of magnitude faster than br-index, 1.9-10x faster than b-move and up to 5.5x faster than the state-of-the-art bi-directional (uncompressed) FM-index columba, which is 36-42x larger. Memory usage (including index size) during APM locate queries is reduced by 1.5x (up to 6.5x) for Hamming distance and 2.5x (up to 7.4x) for edit distance. Move-rb can be constructed 3-14x faster while using 19-141x less memory than br-index, b-move and columba. A variant using a relative Lempel-Ziv-encoded suffix array locates up to 10x faster while being 1.2-2.4x larger. We achieve these speedups by optimizing index operations and search scheme APM algorithms: Without a direction switch, Move-rb computes an all-$k$-character extension in output-optimal $O(k)$ time and a single-character extension in the same time. Augmenting Move-rb with $O((r+\overleftarrow{r})\log(n/r_{\min})\log\sigma)$ bits reduces a single-character extension to $O(\log\sigma)$ time, where $r$ and $\overleftarrow{r}$ are the numbers of runs in the BWT of the text and its reverse, and $r_{\min}=\min(r,\overleftarrow{r})$. A direction switch incurs only $O(\log\log_\omega(n/r_{\min}))$ additional time.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Fischer, Lukas Nalbach

item.title: Faster Sublinear Maximal Independent Set Size
item.description: arXiv:2610.03588v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a sublinear-time algorithm for estimating the size of a maximal independent set in a graph using adjacency-query access with expected running time $\tilde{O}(n^{1+1/3})$, improving over the previous $\tilde{O}(n^{1+1/2})$ bound of Mahadabi et al. [MRTV26]. As a consequence of a reduction of [MRTV26], this also improves the running time for sublinear metric Steiner forest. We further show that a bi-criteria estimate of the $k$-center objective in general metrics can be obtained via a reduction to maximal independent set size estimation.
item.dc:creator: Peter Kiss, Arash Kooroshnezhad

item.title: Stochastic Network Speed Scaling with Competitive Ratios Independent of the Network
item.description: arXiv:2610.03848v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In network speed scaling, jobs arrive over time at a network of servers whose speeds can be tuned, every job must be processed by the servers along one of its allowed routes, and the goal is to minimize the total flow time plus the total energy. For stochastic arrivals, the competitive ratio of Vaze and Nair depends on the network, through the lengths of the routes it uses. We show that this dependence can be removed: we give an algorithm, which routes the jobs by solving a convex program and runs every server at a fixed speed, whose competitive ratio depends only on the power functions; for $P(s)=s^2$, it is at most the golden ratio $\varphi\approx1.618$. The key idea is a lower bound on the optimal cost which, like the cost of our algorithm, is a sum over the servers of a function of each server's load, so the analysis reduces to a single server. We also show that the routing rule of Vaze and Nair can be a factor $\Omega(L)$ away from optimal, where $L$ is the length of the longest route.
item.dc:creator: Yash Khanna

item.title: Attention via Black-Box Vector Search
item.description: arXiv:2610.10135v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse attention mechanisms estimate attention over $n$ tokens using a small subset of keys. Many existing approaches use maximum inner product search (MIPS) to retrieve the heaviest keys, which motivates the following question: given black-box access to a MIPS oracle, how many keys must be retrieved to output an $\varepsilon$-accurate attention estimate? We answer this question by unifying prior approaches through the framework of priority sampling. With a single MIPS index, we show that $\Theta(\sqrt{n}/\varepsilon)$ retrieved keys are both sufficient and necessary. With $\Theta(\log n)$ indices, we give an algorithm that retrieves only $O(\log n+1/\varepsilon^2)$ keys and prove that this is near-optimal. More generally, we design algorithms that establish a smooth tradeoff between the number of MIPS indices and number of retrieved keys. We then show that if we allow augmentation of keys and queries, we can bypass the above lower bounds: there exists a simple priority-sampling estimator using a single MIPS index and $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ retrieved keys. When integrated into LLM inference, our algorithms outperform top-$k$ and sampling approaches used in prior work and yield attention approximation that scales favorably to long contexts.
item.dc:creator: Stepan Zharkov, Krish Singal, Ashwin Padaki, Alexandr Andoni

item.title: Rectangular matrix multiplication from polynomial products
item.description: arXiv:2610.10494v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this note, we extend the matrix-multiplication analysis by OpenAI to rectangular products and prove $\omega(1,k,1)\le2$ for $0\le k\le\frac{1}{2}$, and $\omega(1,k,1)\le1+k+\frac{1}{4k}$ for $k\ge\frac{1}{2}$. In particular, $\omega(1, \frac{1}{2},1)=2$ and the dual exponent satisfies $\alpha\ge\frac{1}{2}$. The proof uses explicit degenerations of convolution tensors, multinomial counting, and Strassen's spectral theorem. An angular constraint on three dot-product parameters gives both the rectangular curve and a bound for $\omega(a,b,c)$. As an application, Zwick's algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths in directed unweighted graphs runs in $O(n^{2.5})$ time. Combining the rectangular bound with the $(\min,+)$-product improvement of Alman and Vassilevska Williams further gives $O(n^{2.4999})$ running time.
item.dc:creator: Przemyslaw Uznanski

item.title: Taxonomic Classification with Tag Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.10500v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Taxonomic classifiers based on exact matches differ in which matches they use and in how each match splits its credit among the taxa containing it: Kraken~2 gives a $k$-mer's credit to the lowest common ancestor of those taxa, SPUMONI~2 labels each position of the read, Tagger gives each maximal exact match (MEM) one label, and Cliffy splits a match's credit evenly over a roughly logarithmic sample of the taxa. We compare these schemes on the same long MEMs, mainly on short 16S rRNA reads classified to genera with SILVA, where credit proportional to the number of occurrences of the MEM in each taxon is the most accurate, by 1.0 to 6.8 percentage points. We compute long MEMs with Boyer--Moore--Li on a run-length compressed suffix array, and count their occurrences in each taxon with a complete, run-length compressed tag array, in time proportional to the number of tag runs in the MEM's BWT interval, without locating any occurrence. We bound the number of tag runs in terms of the BWT runs and of how often suffixes with long common prefixes have different tags, and show that tags constant on $d$ blocks of the text have a macro scheme with at most $r + 2d$ phrases. On SILVA our index takes 1.44\,GB and classifies a read in 66\,$\mu$s with one thread at 93.8\% accuracy, about what Cliffy reports for its 9\,GB index; over minimizer digests it takes 0.49\,GB and reaches 92.5\%, against 84.2\% for Cliffy's digested index on the same reads. On nanopore reads from whole genomes, where almost every long MEM occurs in one species, we instead use each read's longest MEMs, found in one pass of a variant of Boyer--Moore--Li with a $k$-mer filter, which assigns 99.6\% of the reads to their species with no length threshold.
item.dc:creator: Travis Gagie, Gonzalo Navarro

item.title: Subset Sum and Integer Programming Feasibility Test in Near-Optimal Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.12953v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give an $O_{d,\varepsilon}(n+N^{d+\varepsilon})$-time algorithm for multidimensional subset sum on an explicitly listed multiset of $n$ vectors in $[-N,N]^d$, for every fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon>0$. This directly implies an $O_{d,\varepsilon}(n+N^{d+\varepsilon})$-time algorithm for feasibility test of integer programming. Prior to our work, the best-known algorithm has a running time of $O_{d}(n+N^{O(d^2)})$ [Eisenbrand, Weismantel'19]. Specifically, if $d=1$, our algorithm runs in $O_{\varepsilon}(n+N^{1+\varepsilon})$-time for the standard subset sum problem, which is near-linear in the largest input integer. Prior to our work, subset sum can be solved in time near-linear in the target $t$ [Bringmann'17], or near-linear in the mixed parameter $\sqrt{Nt}$ [Chen, Lian, Mao, Zhang'24]. It is a fundamental open problem whether the algorithm can be made near-linear in $N$, which is settled affirmatively in this paper up to an arbitrary small $N^{\varepsilon}$ term.
item.dc:creator: Lin Chen, Yuchen Mao, Guochuan Zhang

item.title: Revenue Maximization in Choice-Based Matching Markets
item.description: arXiv:2411.15727v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The primary contribution of this paper resides in devising constant-factor approximation guarantees for revenue maximization in two-sided matching markets with general pairwise rewards. A major distinction between our work and state-of-the-art results in this context (Ashlagi et al., 2022; Torrico et al., 2023) is that, for the first time, we are able to address reward maximization, reflected by assigning each customer-supplier pair an arbitrarily-valued reward. Our performance guarantees apply to two different settings: the customized model and the inclusive model. The fundamental difference between these settings lies in whether the platform should display to each supplier all selecting customers, as in the inclusive model, or whether the platform can further personalize this set, as in the customized model. Technically speaking, our algorithmic approaches and their analysis revolve around presenting a closely related combinatorial problem, a novel linear relaxation, and developing tailor-made analytical ideas. In both models considered, these ingredients allow us to overcome the lack of submodularity and subadditivity that stems from pairwise rewards, plaguing the applicability of existing methods. We complement our theoretical results with an extensive computational study under different classes of instances where we analyze the empirical reward and running time performance of our proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Dan Nissim, Danny Segev, Alfredo Torrico

item.title: A Framework for the Design of Efficient Diversification Algorithms for Packing and Covering Problems
item.description: arXiv:2501.12261v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: There has been considerable recent interest in computing a diverse collection of solutions to a given optimization problem. Given a classical optimization problem $\Pi$ (e.g., minimum spanning tree, maximum independent set) with input size $n$ and an integer $k\geq 1$, the goal is to generate a collection of $k$ maximally diverse solutions to $\Pi$. This diverse-X paradigm not only allows the user to generate very different solutions, but also helps make systems more secure and robust by handling uncertainty and achieving energy efficiency. For several problems $\Pi$ solvable in polynomial time, there are efficient $\text{poly}(n,k)$-time exact or approximation algorithms available for their diverse-solution variants. In contrast, only FPT algorithms are known for NP-complete problems such as vertex covers and independent sets. In the worst case, these algorithms run in time $\exp((kn)^a)$ for some $a>0$. In this work, we address this gap and give a general framework for $\text{poly}(n,k)$-time \emph{bi-criteria} PTAS for the diverse variants of several NP-hard problems such as \textsc{Knapsack}, \textsc{Maximum Weight Independent Set} (MWIS) and \textsc{Minimum Weight Vertex Cover} (MWVC) in planar graphs. More precisely, given a maximization (or, minimization) problem $\Pi$, an integer $k \geq 1$, user-specified quality threshold $ c \in (0, 1) $, and user-controlled error parameters $\delta,\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, our bi-approximation algorithm returns a collection of $k$ solutions $S_1,S_2,\ldots,S_k$ that are $(1-\delta)c$-optimal and whose diversity is at least a $(1-\varepsilon)$-fraction of the maximum diversity achievable by any collection of $k$ $c$-optimal solutions. To complement our positive results, we prove that the diverse-solution variants of \KP and MWIS mentioned above do not admit standard single-criterion PTASs.

item.title: Sublinear Algorithms for Wasserstein and Total Variation Distances: Applications to Fairness and Privacy Auditing
item.description: arXiv:2503.07775v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Resource-efficiently computing representations of probability distributions and the distances between them while only having access to the samples is a fundamental and useful problem across mathematical sciences. In this paper, we propose a generic framework to learn the probability and cumulative distribution functions (PDFs and CDFs) of a sub-Weibull, i.e. almost any light- or heavy-tailed, distribution while the samples from it arrive in a stream. The idea is to reduce these problems into estimating the frequency of an appropriately chosen subset of the support of a properly discretised distribution. We leverage this reduction to compute mergeable summaries of distributions from the stream of samples while requiring only sublinear space relative to the number of observed samples. This allows us to estimate Wasserstein and Total Variation (TV) distances between any two distributions while samples arrive in streams and from multiple sources. Our algorithms significantly improves on the existing methods for distance estimation incurring super-linear time and linear space complexities, and further extend the mergeable summaries framework to continuous distributions with possibly infinite support. Our results are tight with respect to the existing lower bounds for bounded discrete distributions. In addition, we leverage our proposed estimators of Wasserstein and TV distances to tightly audit the fairness and privacy of algorithms. We empirically demonstrate the efficiency of proposed algorithms across synthetic and real-world datasets.

item.title: Separable convex optimization over indegree polytopes
item.description: arXiv:2509.06182v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study separable discrete convex optimization over indegree vectors of orientations of an undirected graph, focusing on the effect of imposing acyclicity. Since the extreme points of the indegree polytope are precisely the indegree vectors of acyclic orientations, this amounts to comparing optimization over its integer points with optimization over its extreme points. Over all orientations, minimizing a vertex-separable discrete convex objective is strongly polynomial-time solvable by minimum-cost flow. Over acyclic orientations, for every fixed discrete convex function shared by all vertices, we obtain a dichotomy: if the function is linear on the positive integers, the problem is solvable in linear time; otherwise exact optimization is NP-hard on connected simple graphs, and APX-hard when the function is non-negative. We also give strongly polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithms for broad classes of convex and concave objectives. For the $p$-power sum of indegrees, this yields a $2^p$-approximation for every fixed integer $p\geq1$, while the problem is APX-complete for every fixed integer $p\geq2$; if $p$ is part of the input, no deterministic polynomial-time $2^{p^{1-\varepsilon}}$-approximation exists for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. We further give an exact $O(2^{|V|}|V|+\operatorname{poly}(|V|,|E|))$-time dynamic program for general separable objectives, with a matching lower bound in the exponent under the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Finally, decreasingly minimal and increasingly maximal acyclic orientations need not coincide and are both NP-hard, while minimizing the maximum weighted indegree over acyclic orientations remains strongly polynomial-time solvable.

item.title: Elfs, transducers and quantum walks
item.description: arXiv:2605.30013v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electric flow sampling (elfs) is a new tool in the quantum walk toolbox and a useful primitive for solving search, sampling and optimization problems on graphs. We refine this tool by showing that there exists a zero-error transducer for implementing elfs. More broadly, we establish a zero-error transducer for reflecting about the intersection of two subspaces, yielding an errorfree transducer version of the effective gap lemma. Building on this result, we obtain improved quantum walk algorithms for estimating effective resistances and span program witness sizes with an optimal error scaling, and for sampling from the random walk arrival distribution, via the composition of many elfs. Using this last algorithm, we obtain an up-to-quadratic quantum speedup for semi-supervised learning on expander graphs.
item.dc:creator: Simon Apers, J\'er\'emie Roland, Yuxin Zhang

item.title: Tight Approximation Thresholds for Geometric Stabbing
item.description: arXiv:2607.28062v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study geometric covering problems: stabbing axis-parallel squares and cubes by coordinate hyperplanes, stabbing horizontal segments by horizontal and vertical lines, and transversal of separated $d$-intervals. We prove matching NP-hardness bounds for their natural covering-LP thresholds. For every $\varepsilon>0$, square stabbing is NP-hard to approximate within $2-\varepsilon$, horizontal-segment stabbing within $e/(e-1)-\varepsilon$, and, for every fixed $d\ge2$, cube stabbing and separated $d$-interval transversal within $d-\varepsilon$. The results hold with finite candidate sets and when arbitrary admissible lines, hyperplanes, or track points are allowed. We construct harmonic integrality-gap families for squares and cubes and use the Kovaleva--Spieksma gap family for horizontal segments. In each family, every object meets a candidate of every orientation. We lift these gaps through the strict-CSP framework of Kumar, Manokaran, Tulsiani, and Vishnoi, using the Unique Games theorem to obtain NP-hardness. An ordered sampler preserves the LP marginals, coupled shifts make every local sample feasible, and a small perturbation through an absorbing label connects every local support. Cartesian cloning removes rational weights, after which disjoint blocks of candidate coordinates realize each output constraint by one square, cube, or horizontal segment. Applying the same transfer theorem to rectangle-hitting gaps of Pach and Tardos, we prove that stabbing axis-parallel boxes by supplied candidate lines in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is NP-hard to approximate within any fixed constant factor. Incidence-preserving algebraic maps yield the same hardness for hitting boxes in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^6$ by points from supplied finite candidate sets.

item.title: Policy Iteration Is Not Strongly Polynomial for Deterministic Markov Decision Processes: The Price of Algorithmic Anarchy
item.description: arXiv:2609.40147v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We establish exponential iteration lower bounds in the number of states for Howard's policy iteration on deterministic discounted and average-reward Markov decision processes (MDPs), with a constant number of actions per state. This rules out strong polynomiality of Howard's policy iteration in both settings. We further prove that a Dantzig counterpart of Howard's policy iteration runs in strongly polynomial time on deterministic average-reward MDPs. Together with the known strongly polynomial bound for Dantzig's rule on deterministic discounted MDPs, these results establish an exponential separation between the two algorithms in both settings. This separation between Howard's decentralized and simultaneous selfish improvements and Dantzig's coordinated selection of a single action with the largest improvement across all states reveals a ``price'' of algorithmic anarchy.

item.title: W[1]-Hardness of Upper Clique Transversal
item.description: arXiv:2610.04917v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A clique transversal of a graph is a set of vertices intersecting every maximal clique. We prove that deciding whether a graph has an inclusion-wise minimal clique transversal of size at least $k$ is W[1]-hard when parameterized by $k$.
